summary:
An FMJ/FMLink article argues that facility management teams should sequence competing work using Cost of Delay, the economic concept describing how the value of an outcome changes the longer delivery waits. The author frames Cost of Delay as the opportunity cost of waiting, noting that in FM the value at stake may be operational availability, safety exposure, compliance, asset condition or occupant experience rather than only dollars.

A worked example: two failures with similar operational consequence, one needing 30 minutes to fix and one needing 10 minutes, should generally be sequenced shortest first, removing a disruption sooner. But if the longer repair supports an operation with a fixed deadline after which consequences escalate sharply, the order flips. The job did not get shorter; the consequence of waiting got bigger.

The piece criticises conventional priority labels (emergency, urgent, high, medium, low) and SLAs because too much work ends up classified as high priority. Two high items can imply very different decisions: a 20 minute fix that removes meaningful exposure versus a full day job that stays stable until tomorrow. Priority labels communicate importance but not the effect of time; Cost of Delay adds that dimension by combining importance, consequence of waiting and effort required.

The author traces the concept to operations research and product development, crediting Donald Reinertsen for emphasising the economic value of time, later popularised through Lean and Agile. A Maersk Line example from the 2018 Accelerate State of DevOps Report is cited, then carefully caveated as part of a broader transformation.

A table lists delay dimensions: operational, financial, safety and risk, compliance and audit, asset degradation, and stakeholder/reputation. Some costs monetise easily (production line downtime, a hotel room out of inventory); others do not but matter equally. The article closes by noting Cost of Delay is dynamic, rising as audit deadlines approach.

claims.claim: In backlog data examined in the Accelerate State of DevOps Report, three high-value Maersk Line features represented a substantial weekly Cost of Delay
claims.stat: approximately US$7 million per week; 3 features
claims.attribution: 2018 Accelerate State of DevOps Report, cited by the FMJ article

claims.claim: Maersk's reported improvements, including shorter idea-to-release time and faster benefits realization, cannot be attributed to Cost of Delay alone because the transformation also included smaller work items, reduced work in progress, faster feedback and decision-making closer to the work
Donald Reinertsen became particularly influential in product development by emphasizing the economic value of time, with Lean and Agile practices later spreading the reasoning
Operations research has examined the economic sequencing of constrained work for decades, predating modern Agile practices
When two failures impose roughly the same Cost of Delay, the shorter repair should generally be done first
Most facility organizations already classify work as emergency, urgent, high, medium or low, but too many items become high priority

vocabulary: priority classification (emergency, urgent, high, medium, low)
